result:
All 10 tests pass, including the three new ones in `tests/test_t3.py`.

**What I changed**

- Rewrote `editor/buffer.py` from the command pattern to the memento pattern. Each undo step is now a snapshot of the whole buffer text taken before the step. The undo and redo stacks hold strings instead of edit objects.
- Added `transaction()`, `can_undo()`, and `can_redo()`. Every edit, whether a single insert or a whole transaction, now goes through one private commit method that sets the text, pushes the before-snapshot, and clears redo.
- Did not add `apply_plugin` since you said it is the next step. On this design it will be a one-liner that commits the result of calling the plugin on the current text. The last edge check in my run exercised exactly that path with undo and redo.

**Why I switched architectures rather than bolting transactions onto the command pattern**

The previous session picked Approach A, where every edit stores enough to compute its own inverse. That cannot support the new plugin requirement. An opaque `fn(text) -> text` has no inverse, and diffing is disallowed, so the only way to undo it is to have kept the text from before. Once plugin edits need a snapshot anyway, keeping inverse-based commands for insert, delete, and replace would mean two undo mechanisms, which is the special case the team said they do not want. It would also save little memory, since most edits will be plugins. Approach B is explicitly acceptable under the spec, and it makes transactions nearly free: take a snapshot at block start, commit it as the before-state on success, restore it on exception.

**Behavior decisions worth knowing about**

- Transactions nest. An inner block merges into the outer one, but an inner block that raises still rolls back to its own start, so the outer block can catch and continue.
- A step that leaves the text unchanged is not recorded, so an empty transaction or a no-op plugin never creates an undo entry that appears to do nothing.
- Calling undo or redo inside an open transaction raises RuntimeError, because mixing history navigation with an uncommitted block would corrupt the stacks.
- Memory is proportional to buffer size times history length in the worst case, which the spec accepts. Python strings are immutable, so snapshots are references and no copying happens beyond the new string each edit produces. If this ever matters, a history cap is a small addition.

**Repository state**

The buffer, the two newer test files, and `.gitignore` were all untracked before I started and remain uncommitted. Nothing has been committed or staged.
